children: As companies redesign roles and operating models, CHROs are moving from managing job cuts to deciding what workforce comes next

Workforce restructuring is increasingly becoming an organisational-design question rather than simply a headcount exercise. As companies respond to changing business demand, technology adoption, productivity expectations and skills gaps, HR leaders are being drawn deeper into decisions about which roles remain relevant, which skills need to change and where employees can be moved. Professionals Day is observed on September 26; the evolving role of CHROs highlights how workforce decisions are becoming central to organisational strategy.

The shift is particularly relevant as restructuring becomes more closely linked to business-model changes and technology-led redesign. For CHROs, the question is no longer only how many positions need to be removed. It is also whether an existing role can be redesigned, whether an employee can be reskilled or redeployed, and what capabilities the organisation will need after the restructuring.

Recent corporate actions provide the immediate backdrop. Oracle has undertaken another round of workforce reductions in India in September, following an earlier round in 2026. Adidas has confirmed reductions within its India Technology organisation, while PayPal has confirmed that about 220 employees in India were affected by an August workforce reduction. Samsung India has also been reported to have reduced its workforce this year.
For HR leaders, however, these developments raise a wider question: when the structure of an organisation changes, what happens to the people whose roles change with it?
Recent Restructuring Cases

Oracle has undertaken multiple rounds of workforce reductions in India during 2026. A September round was reported to have affected around 3,000 employees across functions including Oracle Health, OCI Security and Oracle Financial Services, following an earlier restructuring exercise that reportedly affected around 12,000 employees in India. The company has been simultaneously increasing investment in AI infrastructure.

Adidas confirmed in September that it was reducing certain roles within its Technology organisation in India to simplify parts of the organisation and align its operating model with changing business requirements. The company said the impact was less than 20 per cent of its India Technology organisation, although media reports had cited a substantially higher figure for its Gurugram technology hub.

PayPal also confirmed that approximately 220 employees, or around 4 per cent of its India workforce, were affected by the 31 August workforce reduction. The company described the changes as part of its previously announced multi-year transformation to simplify global operations.

These cases differ in business context and scale, but they illustrate the broader workforce question facing HR: which work is changing, which capabilities remain important and where can existing employees fit into the next organisational structure?
Restructuring Beyond Costs
Cost remains an important consideration in workforce restructuring, but it is increasingly being combined with questions around productivity, operating models, skills and technology.

Mercer’s Global Talent Trends 2026 finds that 98 per cent of executives expect their organisations to undergo organisational-design changes over the next two years. Planned changes include simplifying reporting lines, centralising governance, flattening organisations, expanding shared services and adopting more flexible workforce models.

AI is adding another layer to this redesign. Ninety-nine per cent of executives surveyed by Mercer expect AI to lead to at least some headcount reduction, while 63 per cent of C-suite respondents identify redesigning work around AI and automation as the people initiative with the greatest potential return on investment.

The implication is that organisations are not simply asking how many employees they need. They are examining what work needs to be performed, how that work should be organised and which skills will be required.

Deloitte India’s ‘Future of Work and People Analytics Maturity – The Indian Story’ also points to a shift in workforce planning. Around 80 per cent of organisations surveyed are strengthening workforce planning and contingent talent strategies, while 76 per cent are actively identifying future skill gaps. More than 60 per cent report a shift from task-based roles towards roles requiring greater problem-solving and creativity.

This places HR closer to the original business decision. As Snigdha Tondapu, Chief Human Resources Officer at Innostax, puts it, "Workforce choices are business choices, so the CHRO belongs in the room before structures are decided." She argues that this requires HR leaders to understand where the business is headed, what capabilities it needs and where the existing structure may be limiting that direction.
Reskill Or Redeploy?
The more difficult decision begins when a role changes but the employee may still have value to the organisation.

A position can become redundant because a process has been automated, a function has been consolidated, or a business model has changed. But the skills behind that position may remain relevant elsewhere.

Mercer’s 2025/2026 Skills Snapshot Survey shows that organisations are moving towards this skills-based approach. Thirty-eight per cent maintain a single enterprise-wide skills library, up from 30 per cent in 2023. Fifty-five per cent map skills directly to jobs, compared with 47 per cent in 2023, while the average proportion of jobs with skills mapped has increased to 72 per cent from 69 per cent in 2023.
For HR, such mapping can provide a basis for deciding whether an employee should be reskilled, moved into another role or exited.

"The question shifts from 'Do they fit today?' to 'Where could they add value as the business evolves?'" says Tondapu. She adds that reskilling or redeployment needs a credible path involving transferable skills, realistic development and an actual vacancy. Where that path does not exist, she says, "an honest exit is fairer to everyone."
Mercer’s Global Talent Trends 2026 reports that 60 per cent of HR leaders expect between 11 and 20 per cent of their workforce to be redeployed or reskilled because of AI within the next two years.

The challenge is therefore to distinguish between a role that has disappeared and a capability that has become obsolete. Employees may possess domain knowledge, customer understanding, technical experience or other transferable skills even when their current positions no longer exist.
HR Moves Upstream
This is also changing when the CHRO enters the restructuring process.

Priyanka Dalvi, Global People Officer at airpay, says the CHRO’s involvement is moving earlier as companies adopt AI, change operating models and rethink how work is performed. "Early involvement also gives organisations more room to reskill or redeploy people, rather than making workforce changes only after a restructuring decision," Dalvi says.

Her point changes the nature of workforce planning. Instead of waiting for a business unit to identify excess positions, HR can model how different operating structures would affect skills, roles and internal mobility before the final structure is established.

Deloitte India’s research reinforces the importance of this capability. Forty-three per cent of organisations surveyed have reached advanced people-analytics maturity, while more than 70 per cent continue to rely on static reporting approaches.

The gap matters because restructuring requires forward-looking information. Historical headcount data can show where an organisation has people; it does not necessarily show which capabilities can be moved into emerging areas.

Mercer reports that 57 per cent of C-suite respondents see improving people analytics as the people initiative that will drive the most return on investment in 2026. Yet only 27 per cent of executives believe HR effectively advises on human-capital risks and opportunities.

For CHROs, the expanded mandate therefore involves workforce scenarios, organisational design, skills intelligence and commercial understanding, alongside the traditional employee-management responsibilities.
The Employees Who Stay
The restructuring decision does not end when roles are removed.

Employees who remain can face changed reporting lines, increased workloads, new responsibilities and uncertainty over whether another round of restructuring could follow. These effects can influence morale, productivity, manager effectiveness and attrition. "The hard part starts after the announcement," Tondapu says. "Workloads need to be reprioritised, not simply passed on to fewer people." She adds that employees need clarity about why the change happened and what comes next, while managers need to remain visible and identify disengagement early.

Mercer’s 2026 findings highlight the broader workforce pressure. Only 44 per cent of employees surveyed said they were thriving, compared with 66 per cent in 2024. Forty per cent were concerned about losing their jobs because of AI, up from 28 per cent in 2024.

This makes the post-restructuring phase an important part of HR strategy. Remaining employees need clarity around changed responsibilities, reporting structures and future skills. Managers also need support because they are often responsible for absorbing additional work while communicating decisions they may not have made themselves.

Internal mobility can become important at this stage. If organisations expect employees to adapt to changing work, they need mechanisms through which people can identify opportunities, build relevant skills and move into emerging roles.
Skills Over Job Titles
Identifying those opportunities requires organisations to look beyond the job title attached to an employee.

Aman Gupta, CHRO, Executive Vice President – CSR, EOHS & Sustainability and Corporate Services, Tata Communications, says organisations need to focus on what employees could do next rather than only what they do today. "A job title tells you what someone does today; a data-driven skill profile can reveal what they could do tomorrow," Gupta says.

This approach can make redeployment more deliberate. Skills inventories, internal mobility systems, cross-functional exposure and skills assessments can help organisations identify employees whose current roles may be shrinking but whose capabilities remain relevant elsewhere.
Gupta says the objective is to match existing capabilities with business needs while creating a pathway towards adjacent or new skills.

That distinction becomes particularly important as restructuring becomes recurring. If organisations repeatedly remove roles without developing internal pathways into emerging positions, they may end up reducing headcount in one area while simultaneously creating shortages in another.
The Future CHRO
The changing nature of restructuring points towards a broader CHRO mandate.

Priyanka Dalvi describes this as a shift from workforce planning towards "workforce sensing" — anticipating how changes in strategy, technology and markets will alter workforce requirements. "The future CHRO will be part strategist, part organisation architect and part change leader," she says, with a focus on continuously aligning people, technology and business outcomes.

Gupta similarly argues that CHROs need stronger workforce and scenario-planning capabilities as technology and industry disruption cycles become shorter. This includes mapping skills, identifying talent gaps and determining whether capabilities should be built internally, acquired, borrowed or redeployed.

Mercer’s findings support this wider shift. Sixty-three per cent of C-suite respondents agree that organisations need skills-powered talent practices, while 53 per cent of employees say they are concerned about having future-ready skills. Sixty-three per cent of employees would trade a 10 per cent pay increase for opportunities to develop AI and digital skills.
For CHROs, the implication is that restructuring can no longer be treated simply as the final stage of a cost programme.

The more strategic question is what the organisation is trying to become after the restructuring. That requires understanding which work remains, which skills are becoming more important, which employees can transition and how the remaining workforce can operate effectively. As restructuring becomes a recurring part of workforce planning, the CHRO role is consequently moving towards workforce architecture — connecting organisational design, skills, internal mobility, scenario planning and change management.
The decision is no longer simply about who leaves. It is about what the organisation needs next, and whether its existing workforce can help build it.
Srijata Dey
